name: Crystal
text: Further, the designer should see the import of the job and be alert to those to whom it is directed, to come to the right choices. Because – like much in life – designing is making choices. Choices from an often large number of possibilities and in the light of an analysis of the job and an idea of the audience. Yet even after this selection there are sufficient possibilities remaining to establish uncertainty. Each choice always shuts out other possibilities. This process of choices has to continue until there remain the essential ingredients, which for the designer at that moment, for that purpose, are essential in coming to the final form.
mark: designing is making choices
citation: Martens, Karel. “What Design Means for Me.” 1990. In Printed Matter / Drukwerk, edited by Robin Kinross, Jaap van Triest, and Karel Martens. London: Hyphen Press, 1996.

name: Crystal
text: I thought this was a really interesting point that connected to both of the excerpts I chose from this week’s readings, especially the idea of looking at the bigger picture and making intentional choices. Karel Martens talks about how designers have to make choices based on the purpose and audience, but there is still uncertainty because every choice creates other possibilities. Juliette’s example made me think about how even something as simple as choosing a colour isn’t necessarily a “right” choice on its own. It depends on the context, the audience, and what you’re trying to communicate. I also saw her points as a good reminder that certain associations aren’t necessarily universal or fixed and often change over time which is important to consider if making design choices based on associations (and maybe not making them based on associations as it won't be very timeless, etc.) Someone also challenged the idea by asking whether choosing not to use blue for a bank to stand out/ differentiate would still be based on the assumption that blue represents trust. Juliette agreed that it is, but said the important thing is being conscious of that association when making the choice. I thought this was interesting because it made me realize that you can’t necessarily avoid existing meanings, you can only be more intentional about how you use or move away from them. This also connected to Erika Hall’s point about looking beyond the immediate user and considering the wider context surrounding a design.
mark: you can only be more intentional about how you use or move away from them
context: She brought up how meanings change and although colours are sometimes linked to certain ideas/ traits (ex.the colour blue is linked to trust and is used by many banks) it can change and it depends on the context. Colour doesn't have an identity and is in itself not a physical tangible thing but a visual perception that differs even between humans and as we age depending on our receptors, etc. Be careful when

name: Leila
text: Thus it seems good to me to formulate the premisses freshly and clearly, so as to reach a form that values content and has respect for the receiver of the message. There is no recipe for this. It is a matter of mentality. It is a process of repeatedly weighing up aims, means and method.
mark: There is no recipe for this.
citation: Martens, Karel. “What Design Means for Me.” 1990. In Printed Matter / Drukwerk, edited by Robin Kinross, Jaap van Triest, and Karel Martens. London: Hyphen Press, 1996.

name: Andrea
text: Word choice matters. Design is the application of intention, and you are only as intentional as you are informed.
mark: you are only as intentional as you are informed
citation: Hall, Erika. “A Design Research Framework.” Mule Design, October 25, 2022. muledesign.com/blog/design-research-framework.

name: Hyunjin
text: “It is important for designers and builders of computer applications to understand the history of transparency, so that they can understand that they have a choice.”
mark: they have a choice
citation: Lialina, Olia. “Once Again, The Doorknob: On Affordance, Forgiveness and Ambiguity in Human-Computer and Human-Robot Interaction.” Contemporary Home Computing, 2018. contemporary-home-computing.org/affordance.

name: Felix
text: Her point and the presentation of Andrew made it even more clear that we should think of AI as a tool and use it appropriately. In his example the AI would have not just come up with this idea, the creative process etc. But AI could be used to supercharge the work and also do things that were not possible before, in this example creating a custom tool that is low cost (time and effort). I agree with this view completely and would like to use the metaphor of a photographer in this case. Just because nowadays "all" people have a smartphone with a camera we still have professional photographers and not everybody suddenly became an expert. I think the same is true for AI and design.
mark: not everybody suddenly became an expert
context: Valerie was agreeing on the point that AI can quickly help you create tools but that you need the knowledge to do so, that Andrew made previously.

name: Yen
text: I like how all of them started the projects from defining the problem, and eventually find out the solution for the problem with systematic way like a researcher. AI for them is a tool that become part of the process, but it seems they all know how they want it to work for them. I think it's like a reminder for me, that if I really want to use AI as a tool for myself, it is important to define the problem precisely, instead of letting it do everything, and it just makes me to have more confident about that, the professionals are most likely not going to be replaced by ai, because they are probably the people who really know how to use them the best.
mark: define the problem precisely, instead of letting it do everything
context: Allen: Presented his new digital product that just launched about chat box, that allows vibe coding in the room, and he would want to hear the feedback from us after a few weeks. Juliette: Presented two of her website renovating projects with different budget scales, by really look into the problem and history of the brand, that she also apply Claude for getting them done with technical parts. Andrew: Presented his project of a unconventional construction book, that he did a big research about tracing back to how color is formed in our eyes, and what exactly RGB is and what CMYK can do with color printing, that eventually he even got to create a tool for testing different color combination for the end printing result.

name: Leila
text: For me, understanding and articulating why something feels right does not come as intuitively as designing something to feel right. But they are two sides of the same coin. There must be a reason. It can be as simple as a particular spring curve or something more innate, like metaphors. Analyzing and making sense of design details beyond just "it feels nice" helps nurture taste, amplify the level of execution, and grow an appreciation for how hard the pursuit of excellence is.
mark: helps nurture taste
citation: Freiberg, Rauno. “Invisible Details of Interaction Design.” Every, July 17, 2023. every.to/p/invisible-details-of-interaction-design.

name: Yen
text: I think what resonated with me the most was his advice on how we should prepare ourselves as designers: we’re not hired just for our taste, but more importantly, for our “context window of taste.” It reminded me of our presentation tomorrow. Michael and Rijk have already reminded us to be prepared to explain the “why” behind our decisions. I think being able to articulate the reasoning behind a design decision, rather than simply relying on intuition, is a really important skill for designers.
mark: explain the “why” behind our decisions
context: Jonathan introduced lots of latest AI tools and recommended us for some reference. He further more answered our questions for him according to careers, ai, and his products.

name: Charitaa
text: This was a super interesting perspective on this because we often hear that since AI can do most things for us, our main job is going to be to use "our good taste" to determine the best outcome and let the machine "handle the rest". But this made me think about how the concept of good taste is also going to evolve with the rest of the industry. Less about having a good visual eye and more about knowing what is actually building and what problems are worth solving. Taste becomes truly useful when it is informed by the context within which it must exist! Example: When you make 100 different prototypes using AI, knowing which versions actually help the target user would be my new definition of having "good taste".
mark: knowing which versions actually help the target user
context: "Taste becomes useful when it is informed by the product and the people using it"

name: Hannah
text: When photography was first developed, I suspect it didn’t seem like an artistic medium because it wasn’t apparent that there were a lot of choices to be made; you just set up the camera and start the exposure. But over time people realized that there were a vast number of things you could do with cameras, and the artistry lies in the many choices that a photographer makes.
mark: the artistry lies in the many choices that a photographer makes
citation: Chiang, Ted. “Why A.I. Isn’t Going to Make Art.” The New Yorker, August 31, 2024. newyorker.com.

name: Fan
text: Art is notoriously hard to define, and so are the differences between good art and bad art. But let me offer a generalization: art is something that results from making a lot of choices.
mark: art is something that results from making a lot of choices
citation: Chiang, Ted. “Why A.I. Isn’t Going to Make Art.” The New Yorker, August 31, 2024. newyorker.com.

name: Crystal
text: art requires making choices at every scale; the countless small-scale choices made during implementation are just as important to the final product as the few large-scale choices made during the conception.
mark: choices at every scale
citation: Chiang, Ted. “Why A.I. Isn’t Going to Make Art.” The New Yorker, August 31, 2024. newyorker.com.

name: Claire
text: An artist—whether working digitally or with paint—implicitly makes far more decisions during the process of making a painting than would fit into a text prompt of a few hundred words.
mark: far more decisions
citation: Chiang, Ted. “Why A.I. Isn’t Going to Make Art.” The New Yorker, August 31, 2024. newyorker.com.

name: Simrin
text: If an A.I. generates a ten-thousand-word story based on your prompt, it has to fill in for all of the choices that you are not making.
mark: it has to fill in for all of the choices that you are not making
citation: Chiang, Ted. “Why A.I. Isn’t Going to Make Art.” The New Yorker, August 31, 2024. newyorker.com.

name: Andrea
text: I think that to be a good designer, we need to maintain control over our work while using AI as a tool rather than letting it make the decisions for us. For example, Jonathan Lee used AI for his presentation slides, but he gave it direction based on his previous work and told it what kind of design to create. In that sense, he was still the one making the creative decisions and using AI to execute or develop his ideas, rather than blindly accepting whatever AI produced.
mark: rather than letting it make the decisions for us
context: He talked about finding a balance between having enough ownership over our work and making sure we don’t feel like AI is doing the work for us.

name: Leila
text: I think this is a very interesting take, because it is true that the general public has access to so many AI technologies right now, and that may become more limited in the future, or need to be paid for. However either way, with AI, humans should take control of the machine rather than the other way around, and choose selectively what we are handing off versus what we are doing ourselves.
mark: choose selectively what we are handing off versus what we are doing ourselves
context: The industry of AI is still being defined, and pricing and access to the technologies will change over time. The point of giving full access right now is to get the general public comfortable with the concept and to get more information from them. However, even with AI, people will always want the direct access to sources and won't hand off all their work.

name: Simrin
text: I agree with this because without knowing how to prompt ai tools to be a coworker and help you design more efficiently is important- you have to have the design knowledge and foundations to intuitively direct the models to generate what you envision.
mark: you have to have the design knowledge and foundations
context: Its about the decisions behind the prompts not necessarily about the tools. We as the designers are the decision makers and make choices for each idea we have - our ability to prompt is what is behind creativity

name: Jasmine
text: The selling point of generative A.I. is that these programs generate vastly more than you put into them, and that is precisely what prevents them from being effective tools for artists.
mark: generate vastly more than you put into them
citation: Chiang, Ted. “Why A.I. Isn’t Going to Make Art.” The New Yorker, August 31, 2024. newyorker.com.

name: Felix
text: Using the example of what is needed to write an app store listing to understand if you have a clear enough vision for your own product, really resonated with me. Especially nowadays that building products has become the easy part there are too many people who do not know what problem they are solving and they should ask themselves that exact question.
mark: building products has become the easy part
context: If you create a product you should be able to write the app store listing, if you cannot do that then you do not know what problem you are solving.

name: Jasmine
text: Jonathan mentioned that "Taste is a collective process. And people can learn engagement by useful and simple experience," while answering the question, "How can we build people’s trust in AI-generated content?" I found this interesting to me because I'm also working on an event discovery and book app in Major Studio class. Based on the interview I did for this project, I found an insight that trustworthy is an important issue, and the decision I did to solve this issue is to provide enough information to build trust. Therefore, his idea of process feedback changed my perspective of how I can make users feel trustworthy.
mark: provide enough information to build trust
context: Taste is a collective process. Useful, simple experiences can learn engagement.

name: Valerie
text: Such a person inadvertently reveals that they think formulating sentences is a nuisance rather than a fundamental part of storytelling in prose. Generative A.I. appeals to people who think they can express themselves in a medium without actually working in that medium. But the creators of traditional novels, paintings, and films are drawn to those art forms because they see the unique expressive potential that each medium affords. It is their eagerness to take full advantage of those potentialities that makes their work satisfying,
mark: express themselves in a medium without actually working in that medium
citation: Chiang, Ted. “Why A.I. Isn’t Going to Make Art.” The New Yorker, August 31, 2024. newyorker.com.

name: Valerie
text: I think this is a statement that rings true now more than ever. The essence of generative AI is to reduce the time it feels like an idiot by making the duration of the task as short as possible. If you create a 4000 word essay with a 100 word prompt, you didn't have to risk feeling like an idiot for another 3900 words. The opportunity for growth was robbed from you. The mark of intelligence is not the ability to produce/reproduce a product; Lord knows we don't need more student essays or vibe coded websites. Intelligence and taste grows through active authorship, not just through passive, ego-free creation.
mark: The opportunity for growth was robbed from you.
context: An important trait in intelligent people is their ability to tolerate being stupid for a more extended period of time. If you can stand feeling stupid for eight hours a day and not go crazy, you could become a rocket scientist. They get bored at knowing what's going on, and jump at opportunities to not know anything.

name: Natay
text: As the linguist Emily M. Bender has noted, teachers don’t ask students to write essays because the world needs more student essays. The point of writing essays is to strengthen students’ critical-thinking skills; in the same way that lifting weights is useful no matter what sport an athlete plays, writing essays develops skills necessary for whatever job a college student will eventually get. Using ChatGPT to complete assignments is like bringing a forklift into the weight room; you will never improve your cognitive fitness that way.
mark: bringing a forklift into the weight room
citation: Chiang, Ted. “Why A.I. Isn’t Going to Make Art.” The New Yorker, August 31, 2024. newyorker.com.

name: Natay
text: I hate thinking about this!!! If we all rely on LMs for all our information, will we all end up with the exact same surface-level understanding and no real depth to our thoughts? Fortunately, there are still people today with deep expertise who serve as our best source of knowledge. But what happens in the future?
mark: the exact same surface-level understanding
context: How do we get access to reality?

name: Linzhuo
text: I found his talk very inspiring, especially the sections on GitHub and Worktrees. I learned a lot of new ways of thinking and interesting perspectives. In the Q&A before the session, I asked him, as a designer, how we should approach the increasingly powerful AI and to what extent we should use it—and whether the effort we put into learning a new software tool might soon be replaced by AI. Design and art are arguably among the first fields to be impacted by the rise of AI. As visual professionals, our aesthetic sensibilities and creative ideas are crucial, yet AI is devouring these distinct styles. By “piecing together” images one by one to blend them seamlessly and treating design concepts as templates, AI produces a vast number of decent visual effects with minimal effort. This is undoubtedly frustrating and confusing for designers. In his talk, Jonathan mentioned that we should “have fun with it.” Rather than constantly fearing that our jobs will be replaced, we should try to use these tools to achieve things we couldn’t do before. Everything has its pros and cons; as one of the first groups to be impacted, we can also become the ones best able to utilize these tools. He also mentioned that we can achieve more by asking AI questions like “How should I try to make this?” I really appreciate his approach to these issues and the advice he offered: taking a more neutral stance when experiencing new things and observing what we can achieve through them.
mark: AI is devouring these distinct styles
context: He discussed how to incorporate AI into our workflow and what mindset to adopt in the face of the rapidly evolving AI industry.

name: Andrea
text: I think this idea is interesting when we relate it to AI, since AI also combines patterns and influences from existing work to generate something new. It raises questions about originality and how we differentiate human creativity from AI. Charita also mentioned that if AI can replicate an artist’s work so closely, what makes us say that human art is better than AI-generated art?
mark: how we differentiate human creativity from AI
context: Art is basically a mix of things that already exist. We take inspiration from other people’s work and ideas then remix them in our own way to create something new. As a painter, she does the work herself, but someone who doesn’t know how to paint might use AI to create the painting they want.

name: Andrea
text: It reduces the amount of intention in the world.
mark: It reduces the amount of intention in the world.
citation: Chiang, Ted. “Why A.I. Isn’t Going to Make Art.” The New Yorker, August 31, 2024. newyorker.com.

name: Crystal
text: I think we are complicit, but it’s hard to feel that way now that AI has become such a normal part of almost everyone work or even in day to day life. When ChatGPT first came out I was very much against it, and as every following agent or assistant came out and more widely used I became a bit more open, and now AI is built into so many tools and everyone uses it that the responsibility feels far removed, even though it’s still there. I think that’s what makes the question important and hard to answer the more normal something becomes, the easier it is to stop questioning the ethics around it since now its seeming okay and "normal"
mark: the responsibility feels far removed, even though it’s still there
context: Asked whether we’re complicit when we use AI to make creative work considering it uses other people's work (ex. all existing Figma files ever) to train on and reference when generating new work.

name: Felix
text: In the words often attributed to Marshall McLuhan (but more properly ascribed to Winston Churchill): 'we shape our tools, and thereafter our tools shape us." We are the technology of our tools: they shape and form us. Our tools have agency, and thus a claim upon the more-than-human world as well.
mark: we shape our tools, and thereafter our tools shape us
citation: Bridle, James. Ways of Being: Animals, Plants, Machines: The Search for a Planetary Intelligence. New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2022, 18.
